Copilot Readiness

Defence in Depth

Top Risks

  1. AU-008 Every administrator has a phishing-resistant method registered Critical 3 affected The phishing-resistant policy for administrators (CA-003) can only be enforced once every administrator has a method that satisfies it. This check is the readiness gate: who still signs in with a push notification or a code that an adversary-in-the-middle kit can relay.
  2. CA-002 MFA required for all users Critical 1 affected A tenant-wide MFA policy is the baseline every other control assumes. Per-user MFA and security defaults cover fewer scenarios and cannot be scoped or reported on. Every account excluded from the policy is an account that signs in with a password alone, which is why the check counts a policy as passing only when its exclusions are limited to the break-glass accounts.
  3. CA-003 Phishing-resistant authentication for administrator roles Critical 11 affected Push notifications and one-time codes can be relayed by an adversary-in-the-middle kit, which captures the session as soon as the administrator approves. Phishing-resistant methods bind the credential to the site, so the relayed prompt fails. Administrators are the accounts those kits are aimed at, and the roles listed here are the ones Microsoft recommends protecting first.
  4. AU-001 SMS and voice disabled or scoped to a migration group High SMS and voice are the weakest second factors: SIM swaps, SS7 interception and social engineering of carriers all defeat them, and they cannot be made phishing-resistant. Leaving them enabled for all users means an attacker who needs a second factor picks the easiest one.
  5. AU-006 MFA registered for every member High An MFA policy only protects users who have a method registered; the rest are prompted to register at their next sign-in, which an attacker with the password is happy to do. The registered percentage is the real coverage number behind every MFA policy.

C17: Deployed-ahead cannot be dated without the oversharing baseline (see C3); Copilot status in the profile is 'pilot'.

Restricted access control, restricted content discovery and restricted SharePoint search are stopgaps: they let Copilot be turned on while site owners clean up. The end state is correct permissions, labels that encrypt the top tier, and reviews that keep both true.

71 finding(s) to fix and 34 improvement(s), most urgent first. Within each priority the quick fixes come first, then what affects the most. Each card has the steps, the portal page and the Microsoft Learn article.

Do Today 42

Quick fixes that users will not notice or will barely notice: a setting each, under an hour. The most severe first.

  • High EP-021 Defender Antivirus active on every deviceDefender takes over in the background; a device with another antivirus may need that one removed.
  • High EP-020 Defender sensors healthy: none inactive or impaired over 7 daysFixing sensors happens in the background, sometimes with a restart.
  • High OP-006 Nothing on the expiry calendar within the warning windowNo user change if renewed in time; a missed renewal breaks the app or device it covers.
  • High CA-012 Break-glass accounts excluded from every blocking policyOnly the emergency accounts are affected; users see nothing.
  • High CA-013 No policy references a deleted objectUsers who fell inside or outside a policy because of the deleted object go back to the intended controls.
  • High DEV-008 Apple push certificate and VPP tokens well before expiryAn admin renewal users never see, as long as it is done before the date.
  • High CP-004 Default sharing link is Specific peopleThe share dialog starts at Specific people; users change it when they mean to.
  • High EM-001 EOP preset security policy assigned to everyoneMore suspicious mail goes to quarantine; users get a quarantine notice for the mail they might want.
  • High EM-002 Defender for Office 365 preset policy assigned to everyoneLinks in mail are checked when clicked, and some attachments arrive a minute later after scanning.
  • High EP-030 Local administrators cannot add their own Defender exclusionsA person with local administrator rights can no longer exclude a folder from scanning by themselves.

Control Chains

Some controls protect only when the others in their chain hold. A chain breaks at its first failing link; fix that link first.

Broken at DEV-015 2 of 3 links hold

A device under attack loses access

  1. PassDEV-012 Defender for Endpoint connector enabled in IntuneDefender tells Intune how risky each device is
  2. FailDEV-015 Compliance policies require a Defender device risk levelCompliance turns that risk into a noncompliant verdict
  3. PassCA-005 Compliant device required for Office 365 on Windows and macOSSign-in to Office 365 needs the compliant verdict

Requiring a compliant device only helps if compliance knows when a device is compromised. Defender has to report risk to Intune, compliance has to act on it, and Conditional Access has to require compliance. With any link missing, an infected laptop keeps its access to Microsoft 365.

Broken at AU-006 1 of 3 links hold

A risky sign-in is challenged and a compromised account is contained

  1. FailAU-006 MFA registered for every memberUsers can answer the challenge when it comes
  2. FailCA-004 Risk-based policies for sign-in risk and user riskRisky sign-ins and risky users are challenged or blocked
  3. PassID-015 No high-risk users left unaddressedSomeone works the detections that remain

Entra ID Protection detects leaked credentials and unusual sign-ins, but only Conditional Access acts on them, and the response is an MFA challenge or a password change the user must be able to complete. Users without MFA registered get blocked or, worse, the policy is relaxed. Detections nobody works stay open.

Broken at CP-013 2 of 3 links hold

Copilot cannot surface what was overshared

  1. PassCL-015 No site shared with Anyone links or Everyone grants beyond the thresholdExposure is cut back first, so less is reachable
  2. PassPV-002 Sensitivity labels defined and published to all usersSensitive content can be marked as such
  3. FailCP-013 DLP policy for the Copilot locationCopilot is kept away from what is marked

Copilot answers from everything the user can open. Exposure has to be reduced first, sensitive content has to be labelled, and DLP has to stop Copilot from processing what is labelled. Labels without DLP, or DLP over content shared with everyone, leave the gap open.

CA-003 Phishing-resistant authentication for administrator roles

What We Found
  • Admin roles covered by phishing-resistant MFA: 3
  • Admin roles in scope: 14

11 affected.

Affected (11)
  • Application Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Authentication Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Billing Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Cloud Application Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Conditional Access Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Helpdesk Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Password Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Privileged Authentication Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • Privileged Role Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • SharePoint Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
  • User Administrator (no enabled policy requires phishing-resistant MFA for this role)
Why It Matters

Push notifications and one-time codes can be relayed by an adversary-in-the-middle kit, which captures the session as soon as the administrator approves. Phishing-resistant methods bind the credential to the site, so the relayed prompt fails. Administrators are the accounts those kits are aimed at, and the roles listed here are the ones Microsoft recommends protecting first.

How To Fix
  1. Issue passkeys or FIDO2 keys to every administrator and have them register (AU-008).
  2. Create an enabled policy that targets the privileged directory roles for all cloud apps and grants access only with the built-in Phishing-resistant MFA authentication strength.
  3. Keep the break-glass accounts on a separate policy with the same strength.

What users notice: Administrators sign in with a passkey or security key; push and code approvals stop working for admin roles.

What We Found

Affected (3)

  • casey.ingram@fernquill.example (registered: Microsoft Authenticator (push), Authenticator app code)

Why It Matters

The phishing-resistant policy for administrators (CA-003) can only be enforced once every administrator has a method that satisfies it. This check is the readiness gate: who still signs in with a push notification or a code that an adversary-in-the-middle kit can relay.

How To Fix
  1. Issue a hardware key or a device-bound passkey to each administrator listed and have them register it.
  2. Once every administrator has registered, enforce the phishing-resistant strength for admin roles (CA-003). Before that, the policy would lock them out.

What users notice: Each administrator registers a hardware key or a passkey, about ten minutes once.

CA-002 MFA required for all users

What We Found
  • Policies requiring MFA for all users: 0

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • CA-002-Users-Require MFA for all cloud apps (excludes more than break-glass: BreakGlass-01, BreakGlass-02, CA-Exclude-ServiceAccounts, CA-Exclude-MFA-Legacy)
Why It Matters

A tenant-wide MFA policy is the baseline every other control assumes. Per-user MFA and security defaults cover fewer scenarios and cannot be scoped or reported on. Every account excluded from the policy is an account that signs in with a password alone, which is why the check counts a policy as passing only when its exclusions are limited to the break-glass accounts.

How To Fix
  1. Create an enabled policy for all users and all cloud apps that requires multifactor authentication or an authentication strength.
  2. Exclude only the break-glass accounts.
  3. Move service accounts to workload identities or managed identities instead of excluding them.
  4. Move any legacy exclusion group into a scoped policy with an end date.

What users notice: Every user answers MFA when they sign in, then not again on the same device for a while.

Why It Matters

One calendar for every expiry that takes a service down: application secrets, SAML signing certificates, the Apple push certificate, VPP and Automated Device Enrollment tokens, trial subscriptions, subscriptions in their grace period, and the token-signing certificate of each federated domain, which stops every sign-in in that domain the day it lapses.

How To Fix

Renew each listed item before its date: rotate the application credential, roll the SAML certificate, renew the Apple push certificate, VPP token or Automated Device Enrollment token, buy or let go the trial or the subscription that is in its grace period, and make sure the federation server has rolled its token-signing certificate and Entra has picked the new one up. CA-012 Break-glass accounts excluded from every blocking policy

What We Found
  • Break-glass accounts named in the profile: yes
  • Block policies that include the break-glass accounts: 2

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • Block legacy authentication (blocks access without excluding a break-glass account or group)
  • CA-007-Users-Register security info from trusted locations (blocks access without excluding a break-glass account or group)
Why It Matters

A blocking policy that applies to the break-glass accounts can lock every administrator out of the tenant at once, typically during the incident the policy was written for. A policy misfire, an MFA outage or a mistaken location change then has no way back in. Excluding the emergency accounts from every Block is what keeps Conditional Access recoverable.

How To Fix
  1. Name the break-glass accounts in the profile and keep them in a dedicated group.
  2. Exclude that group from every policy with a Block control.
  3. Protect the accounts with a separate phishing-resistant policy and alert on their sign-ins.
  4. Test one of them every quarter.

What users notice: Only the emergency accounts are affected; users see nothing.

CA-013 No policy references a deleted object

What We Found
  • Policies referencing deleted objects: 2

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • CA-005-Users-Require compliant device for Windows and macOS (References a deleted group: 22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222299. The policy silently no longer covers or excludes it.)
  • CA-007-Users-Register security info from trusted locations (References a deleted namedLocation: 55555555-5555-5555-5555-555555555599. The policy silently no longer covers or excludes it.)
Why It Matters

When a group, user or named location a policy references is deleted, the policy keeps the orphaned id and silently stops covering or excluding whoever it pointed at. The portal shows nothing wrong. The result is a policy that reads correctly and does something different, which is the worst kind of drift.

How To Fix
  1. Open each policy listed and find the assignment, location or strength that no longer resolves.
  2. Replace or remove it.
  3. If the deleted object was an exclusion group, check who was in it, because those accounts are now inside the policy (or outside it, if it was an include).

What users notice: Users who fell inside or outside a policy because of the deleted object go back to the intended controls.

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • CA-002-Users-Require MFA for all cloud apps (skips MFA from: All trusted locations (built-in))
Why It Matters

Skipping MFA from the office network treats the network as the credential. Anyone on the wireless, a compromised device on the LAN, or a VPN session from a stolen laptop then signs in with a password alone. Zero trust guidance drops the location bypass because the perimeter is the easiest control to get behind.

How To Fix
  1. Remove the trusted-location exclusion from the MFA policies listed.
  2. Where a specific system needs a location exclusion, scope it to that application and record the exception with an owner and an expiry.

Why It Matters

A subscription past its term is in a grace period first, then suspended, then deleted with its data. The security features go with it: Conditional Access with Entra ID P1, Defender, Intune. What We Found

Why It Matters

With merge allowed, an exclusion added on the device joins the ones from policy. The first thing a good deal of malware does with administrator rights is exclude its own folder, and a developer in a hurry does the same. Turning merge off makes the policy the only source of exclusions.

How To Fix
  1. In Intune, Endpoint security, Antivirus, open your Microsoft Defender Antivirus policy for Windows, or create one.
  2. Set Disable Local Admin Merge to Enable.

Why It Matters

Every member of an exclusion group is outside the policy entirely. CA-004 Risk-based policies for sign-in risk and user risk

What We Found
  • Sign-in risk policies: 0
  • User risk policies: 0
Why It Matters

Identity Protection scores sign-ins and users on leaked credentials, anonymous networks, impossible travel and attacker infrastructure. Without a policy that acts on the score, the detections are a report nobody reads until after the incident. Requiring MFA on risky sign-ins and a password change on risky users turns the detection into an automatic response.

How To Fix
  1. Create a policy for all users and all cloud apps that requires multifactor authentication for medium and high sign-in risk.
  2. Create a second policy that requires multifactor authentication and a secure password change for high user risk.
  3. Exclude the break-glass accounts from both.
  4. Run both in report-only mode for a week, watch the Identity Protection reports, then enable them.

What users notice: A user whose sign-in looks risky gets an extra MFA prompt; one whose account looks compromised changes their password.

PP-005 Tenant isolation is on in Power Platform

What We Found
  • Tenant isolation is on: no
Why It Matters

A connector signs in wherever its maker has an account. Without isolation a flow in your tenant can sign in to a personal or a competitor's tenant and copy data there, and a flow in someone else's tenant can sign in to yours with one of your users' accounts. Isolation stops both unless you name the tenant.

How To Fix
  1. In the Power Platform admin center, open Policies, Tenant isolation (newer menus: Security, Identity and access).
  2. Find the connections that cross tenants today, with the cross-tenant connection report.
  3. Turn isolation on and add the tenants you work with to the allow list, with the direction each needs.

What users notice: A connection that signs in to another organisation's tenant, or one from another tenant into yours, stops working unless that tenant is on the allow list.

What We Found

Affected (2)

  • Mailbox Archiver: Mail.ReadWrite (application permission granted 12/16/2024 09:00:00)
Why It Matters

An application permission applies to every mailbox, site or user in the tenant with no user present. Directory.ReadWrite.All or Mail.ReadWrite on a forgotten app is a complete data exfiltration path that bypasses Conditional Access entirely. Each one should have a name next to it.

How To Fix
  1. For each grant listed, confirm the workload still exists and needs that permission.
  2. Replace tenant-wide permissions with resource-specific consent or a narrower permission, and remove the rest.
  3. Record the surviving grants as exceptions with an owner and a review date.

EP-026 Defender Antivirus scans archives, mail, scripts, removable drives and network files

What We Found
  • A policy turns on archive scanning: yes
  • A policy turns on email scanning: yes
  • A policy turns on script scanning: yes
  • A policy scans removable drives in a full scan: no
  • A policy scans files on the network: no

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • removable drives in a full scan (no assigned policy turns this scan on)
  • files on the network (no assigned policy turns this scan on)
Why It Matters

Malware arrives zipped, attached to mail, as a script, on a USB stick or from a file share. Each of these is a separate switch in Defender Antivirus, and two of them, mail and removable drives, are off until a policy turns them on. The others are on by default, which a local administrator can change unless a policy sets them. The scans listed are set by no assigned policy.

How To Fix
  1. In Intune, Endpoint security, Antivirus, open your Microsoft Defender Antivirus policy for Windows, or create one.
  2. Set Allow Archive Scanning, Allow Email Scanning, Allow Script Scanning, Allow Full Scan Removable Drive Scanning and Allow Scanning Network Files to Allowed.
  3. Assign the policy to all Windows devices.

What users notice: A full scan takes a little longer on a device with a large USB drive attached.

ID-023 Admin command-line tools open only to the people who need them

What We Found
  • Admin command-line tools anyone can sign in to: 2

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • Microsoft Azure CLI (anyone can sign in: assignment not required)
  • Microsoft Azure PowerShell (anyone can sign in: assignment not required)
Why It Matters

Any member can sign in to Graph PowerShell, Graph Explorer, the Azure CLI or the Exchange, SharePoint and Teams shells and read whatever their account can see: the whole directory, groups, devices and much of the configuration. Attackers with a stolen password or token use exactly these tools, because they are trusted Microsoft apps with consent already in place. Limiting them to the people who need them removes a ready-made reconnaissance kit from every ordinary account.

How To Fix
  1. For each tool listed, open its enterprise application (create it first with New-MgServicePrincipal -AppId <id> if the tenant has none yet), set Assignment required to Yes, and assign a group of the administrators and developers who use it, including the account that runs TenantKeep Posture.
  2. Or block the tools in Conditional Access for everyone except that group; for Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, blocking Windows Azure Service Management for everyone else does the same.
  3. Note that Restrict access to Microsoft Entra admin center only hides the portal: it does not stop PowerShell or Graph.

What users notice: Only people outside the assigned group notice: Graph PowerShell, the Azure CLI and the other shells refuse their sign-in. Most users never run them.

2 affected.

Affected (2)

  • Certificates (no maximum lifetime)
Why It Matters

The portal offers two years for a secret and lets a script ask for a hundred. A credential nobody has to renew is one nobody remembers, and it keeps working long after the person who made it has left. A maximum lifetime turns every credential into something that is looked at again.

How To Fix
  1. In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Security, Application policies.
  2. Open Restrict max password lifetime and Restrict max certificate lifetime, set each to On for all applications, with about half a year for secrets and a year for certificates.

What users notice: Nothing changes for users. Whoever looks after an application renews its secret or certificate on a schedule.

  • Platforms not requiring a device risk level: 1

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • Android (no assigned compliance policy requires a Defender device risk level)
Why It Matters

Defender for Endpoint scores each device's risk from what it sees on the machine. A compliance policy can require that score to be Low or Clear, which is how an attack in progress cuts the device off from Microsoft 365 until it is cleaned up. The setting is per platform and off by default.

How To Fix
  1. Turn on the Defender for Endpoint connector in Intune with compliance policy evaluation for each platform (DEV-012).
  2. In each platform's assigned compliance policy, open Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and set Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score to Low or Clear.
  3. Set the policy's actions for noncompliance to mark the device noncompliant immediately, then watch the compliance report for a day before relying on it.

What users notice: A device with an active threat loses access to Microsoft 365 until it is cleaned; users of healthy devices notice nothing.

What We Found
  • Certificate connectors not connected: 1
  • Certificate connector, days without contact: 3

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • Certificate Connector on FQ-PKI02 (last heard from 2026-11-04, inactive)
Why It Matters

The certificate connector is a Windows server on the network that hands certificates from the organisation's own certificate authority to Intune devices. Nothing in the cloud says when it stops, and the first sign is a device that cannot join the Wi-Fi weeks later. A connector Intune calls inactive, or one not heard from for days, is listed. A tenant with no connector passes: there is nothing to lose.

How To Fix
  1. On each server listed, check that the Intune certificate connector services are running and that the server can reach Intune.
  2. Look at the connector's event log (Applications and Services Logs, Microsoft, Intune, CertificateConnectors) for why it stopped.
  3. Sign the connector in again or reinstall it, and remove from Intune any connector whose server is gone.

What users notice: While a connector is down no device gets a new or renewed certificate, so Wi-Fi, VPN and email that sign in with one stop working as certificates run out.

What We Found

  • Bulk complaint level, highest allowed: 6

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • Default (bulk threshold 7 (limit 6))
Why It Matters

The default anti-spam policy ships looser than Microsoft's own recommendation: a bulk threshold of 7, and high-confidence spam sent to Junk where one click opens it. Each value here is one where the Standard preset is stricter than the default, so a policy that still has the default lets through what Microsoft itself would hold.

How To Fix
  1. The simplest fix is to assign the Standard preset security policy to everyone (EM-001): it sets every value below and keeps them current.
  2. Otherwise, in the Defender portal open Email & collaboration, Policies & rules, Threat policies, Anti-spam, and edit each listed policy.
  3. Bulk threshold 6 or lower and bulk marked as spam; spam and bulk to Junk or Quarantine; high-confidence spam and phishing to Quarantine; quarantine kept 30 days; safety tips on; the advanced spam filter options off.

What users notice: More junk lands in Junk or quarantine and less in the inbox. People release their own spam from quarantine if the quarantine policy lets them.

1 affected.

Affected (1)

Why It Matters

Impersonation protection finds the message that claims to be the finance director from a look-alike address. Left at its defaults the policy takes no action on it, and a trusted sender or domain entry tells it never to look. The detections only count when the policy does something with them.

How To Fix
  1. The simplest fix is to assign the Standard preset security policy to everyone (EM-002).
  2. Otherwise, in the Defender portal open Anti-phishing and edit each listed policy: phishing email threshold 3 (More aggressive) or higher.
  3. Under Actions, quarantine a message that impersonates a protected person or domain, and move or quarantine one mailbox intelligence flags.
  4. Empty the trusted senders and domains unless each entry has an owner and a reason.

What users notice: A message that pretends to be an executive or a look-alike of your domain goes to quarantine and not to Junk.

CA-016 Device code sign-in blocked

What We Found
  • Policies that block device code sign-in for everyone: 0
Why It Matters

Device code phishing is a sign-in on the attacker's behalf: the attacker starts a device code sign-in with a trusted app, sends the code to a user as an urgent request, and the user signs in with MFA on the real Microsoft page, handing the attacker a token. MFA does not stop it because the user completes MFA. Few organisations need device code sign-in at all, so blocking it closes the attack for almost no cost.

How To Fix
  1. Create a Conditional Access policy for all users and all resources with the condition Authentication flows, Device code flow (and Authentication transfer), and the grant Block access.
  2. Exclude only the break-glass accounts and a group for devices that really need device code sign-in (meeting room displays, some command-line work), and keep that group small.
  3. Start in report-only mode for a week and check the sign-in log for device code sign-ins you did not expect.

What users notice: Almost no one notices. People who type a code at microsoft.com/devicelogin to sign in a TV, a shared display or a command-line tool are refused unless they are in the exception group.

Why It Matters

One Intune administrator session can wipe every device, or push a script to every device, in a few clicks. Attackers who take such a session have done exactly that. The check passes when at least one approval policy exists, and the facts say which kinds of change the policies cover.

How To Fix

  2. Start with the profile types that can do the most harm at once: device actions such as wipe and retire, scripts, and role changes.

Why It Matters

An expired credential on a live integration is an outage waiting for the next token refresh. Expired credentials left in place also hide which ones are actually in use. Thirty days is the window in which rotation can be scheduled rather than done in an incident.

Affected (2)
  • Mailbox Archiver (1 Graph permission(s): Mail.ReadWrite, no sign-in on record)
  • Timesheet Export (1 Graph permission(s): User.Read.All, last sign-in 2026-04-18)
Why It Matters

An application permission works with no user present, for as long as the application has a credential. An application that has not signed in for months and still holds permissions on Microsoft Graph is access nobody is watching: its secret can be in an old script, a retired server or a former supplier's hands. Applications made in the last 90 days are too new to judge and are left out.

How To Fix
  1. For each application listed, find its owner and ask whether it is still in use.
  2. Remove the application permissions of one that is not, or delete its enterprise application and app registration.

What users notice: None for an application nobody uses. One that runs once a year stops the next time it runs if its permissions were removed, so ask first.

Why It Matters

An owner is the technical contact for an agent: the one who can change its credentials, see what it is doing and switch it off. An agent with no owner keeps its access, and nobody is placed to notice when it is misused or no longer needed. This check counts the owners on agent identities, on agent blueprints and on the blueprints' service principals. It does not tell an owner whose account is disabled from one who is still here.

What We Found

  • Kinds of passkey named in the key restrictions: 0
Why It Matters

Without key restrictions any FIDO2 authenticator can be registered, a cheap key with poor protection for its secret or a passkey synced to a personal password manager among them. A list of the keys you accept is how you know what your phishing-resistant sign-ins actually rest on. The check counts how many kinds of key are named, not which.

How To Fix

What We Found

Why It Matters

Token protection binds the sign-in token to the device it was issued to, so a session cookie copied from a phished or malware-infected machine stops working elsewhere. It closes the gap that MFA leaves open once the user has already signed in. Client support is still growing, which is why report-only with a date counts here.

How To Fix
  1. Create a policy for all users targeting Exchange Online and SharePoint Online on the Windows platform with the session control Require token protection for sign-in sessions, in report-only mode.

What We Found
  • Policies that end the browser session on unmanaged devices: 0
  • Policies that set a sign-in frequency for unmanaged devices: 0
Why It Matters

A browser on a home or hotel computer keeps a session for weeks unless told otherwise, and the next person at that keyboard, or malware that copies the cookie, has the mailbox. On a device you manage you can protect the session; on one you do not, the only control is to make it short.

How To Fix
  1. Create a Conditional Access policy for all users and all resources with a device filter that picks out unmanaged devices (for example, include devices where isCompliant is not True).
  2. Under Session, set Persistent browser session to Never persistent and Sign-in frequency to a number of hours.
  3. Start in report-only mode and exclude the break-glass accounts.

What users notice: On a personal or shared computer people are not offered to stay signed in, and sign in again after the hours you set.

What We Found
  • Agent identities in the tenant: 3
  • Policies that block agent identities: 0
  • Agents' user accounts in the tenant: 1

Why It Matters

An agent gets tokens with no person, device or second factor involved, so the policies written for people do not apply to it. Conditional Access treats agent identities and agents' user accounts as kinds of their own, and until a policy names them every token request from an agent is allowed. Microsoft's pattern is to block all agents except the ones you have approved. This check looks for an enabled policy that blocks, for each of the two kinds the tenant has.

How To Fix
  1. Create a Conditional Access policy assigned to agents, all agent identities, with Grant set to Block access, and exclude the agents you have approved by a custom security attribute or by name.
  2. Create a second policy for agents' user accounts (Users, All agent users) in the same way. They are a kind of their own and the first policy does not reach them.
  3. Run both report-only first and read the sign-in log for the agents they would have stopped.

What users notice: Nothing changes for people. An agent nobody approved stops getting tokens.

EM-028 Direct Send is rejected

What We Found
  • Direct Send rejected: no
Why It Matters

Direct Send lets anything on the internet hand mail to your tenant's own endpoint with no sign-in, saying it is from one of your own addresses. It was meant for printers. It is also how a message that claims to be from your finance director reaches a mailbox without passing your sender checks the way outside mail does. With it rejected, mail from your own domains has to come through a connector or a signed-in sender.

How To Fix
  1. Find what sends mail to your own domains without signing in: printers, scanners, line-of-business applications and outside services that send as your domain.
  2. Give each one a way that still works: SMTP client submission with a mailbox, or a partner inbound connector that matches its certificate or its address.
  3. Then turn Direct Send off: Set-OrganizationConfig -RejectDirectSend $true. It takes about half an hour to apply.
  4. Watch the message trace for rejected mail for a week and add a connector for anything that was missed.

What users notice: A printer or application that sends unauthenticated mail as your own domain with no connector stops delivering until it has one.

ID-028 New client secrets are refused on applications

What We Found
  • New client secrets are refused: no
Why It Matters

A client secret is a password for an application: it sits in a configuration file, a pipeline variable or a script, and it works from anywhere with no MFA. An attacker with rights over an application adds a secret of their own and keeps the access after the person they phished changes a password. Refusing new secrets closes both.

How To Fix
  1. In the Entra admin center, open Enterprise apps, Security, Application policies.
  2. Open Block password addition, set it to On for all applications, and leave the date empty so older applications are covered too.
  3. Move the applications that still use a secret to a certificate or a federated credential first, or give the few that cannot move an exception policy of their own.

What users notice: Nothing changes for users. A developer who tries to add a client secret is refused and uses a certificate or a federated credential.

How To Fix

  2. Promote it to enforcement.

What users notice: Some files get a label automatically, which can add encryption or a watermark.

ID-043 App registrations sign in with certificates, not client secrets

What We Found
  • App registrations with a client secret: 2

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • Drawing Vault Sync (1 client secret(s))
  • Timesheet Export (2 client secret(s))
Why It Matters

A client secret is a password for an application: a string that works from anywhere, gets pasted into configuration files and pipelines, and is as good as the application's permissions to whoever finds it. A certificate's private key can stay in a vault or on the machine, and a managed identity has no credential to leak. The applications listed still hold a secret.

How To Fix
  1. For each application listed, ask its owner how it signs in. A workload in Azure should use a managed identity and needs no credential at all.
  2. Elsewhere, add a certificate to the registration or a federated credential for the platform it runs on, switch the application to it, then delete the secret.
  3. Stop new ones: the tenant app management policy can block new secrets (ID-028).

What users notice: Nothing changes for people. Each application's owner has a change to make.

CA-015 Policy names follow the naming convention

What We Found
  • Policies off the naming convention: 2
  • Policy name pattern: ^CA-\d{3}-

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • Block legacy authentication (does not match ^CA-\d{3}-)
  • Sign-in risk: require MFA (report-only pilot) (does not match ^CA-\d{3}-)
Why It Matters

A naming convention is what lets a reviewer read a policy list and know what each policy is for without opening it. Tenants whose policies are named by whoever created them tend to have duplicates and gaps nobody noticed. With a pattern in the profile the check enforces it; without one it looks for a prefix-and-number structure across the names, and free-text names are the finding.

How To Fix
  1. Adopt a convention such as CA-<number>-<persona>-<control>; the Conditional Access document's naming report proposes a name for each policy.
  2. Rename the policies listed.
  3. Record the pattern in the profile (thresholds.namePattern) so the check enforces that exact pattern from then on.

What users notice: Renaming policies changes nothing users see.

1 affected.

Why It Matters

A disabled agent cannot sign in, but it still holds its permissions, its roles and its place in groups, and turning it back on restores all of them at once. Left for months, nobody remembers what it was for or whether the reason it was stopped still stands. This check lists agent identities and blueprints' service principals that are disabled.

CA-018 Authentication transfer blocked

What We Found
  • Policies that block authentication transfer for everyone: 0
Why It Matters

Authentication transfer hands a signed-in session from a computer to a phone through a QR code. It skips the checks a fresh sign-in on the phone would meet, the device check among them, and a person can be talked into scanning a code that signs an attacker's phone in. Few organisations depend on it.

How To Fix
  1. Open the Conditional Access policy that blocks device code sign-in (CA-016), or create one for all users and all resources.
  2. Under Conditions, Authentication flows, tick Authentication transfer as well, with the grant Block access.
  3. Exclude only the break-glass accounts.

What users notice: People can no longer scan a QR code in a desktop app to sign in the same app on a phone. They sign in on the phone itself.

ID-034 Administrators cannot reset their own password by self-service

What We Found
  • Administrators can reset their own password by self-service: yes
Why It Matters

Self-service reset for an administrator is a second way into the most powerful accounts in the tenant, and it is guarded by a phone number and a mailbox, not by the sign-in rules you wrote for administrators. Sending those resets through another administrator puts a person in the path.

How To Fix
  1. The admin center has no switch for this.
  2. With Microsoft Graph PowerShell, as a Global Administrator: Update-MgPolicyAuthorizationPolicy -AllowedToUseSspr:$false
  3. Make sure at least two administrators can reset each other's passwords, and that the break-glass accounts are tested.

What users notice: An administrator who forgets a password asks another administrator to reset it.

ID-041 People do not read their own BitLocker keys by self-service

What We Found
  • People can read the BitLocker keys of their own devices: yes
Why It Matters

The recovery key unlocks the disk without the PIN or the person. If the owner can read it from their account, so can anyone who has taken over that account and has the laptop, which is the stolen-laptop case BitLocker exists for.

How To Fix
  1. In the Entra admin center, open Devices, Device settings.
  2. Set Restrict users from recovering the BitLocker key(s) for their owned devices to Yes.
  3. Make sure the help desk can look up a key and has a way to check who is asking.

What users notice: Someone locked out of a laptop asks the help desk for the recovery key and no longer looks it up from another device.

UX-004 Windows settings backup and restore turned on

What We Found
  • Windows settings restore on: no
Why It Matters

Windows settings backup and restore brings a person's settings and pinned apps to a replacement device during setup. It is off until an administrator turns it on, and it makes a device swap feel like the same machine.

How To Fix
  1. In Intune, Devices, Enrollment, Windows, select Windows Backup and Restore and set Show restore page to On.
  2. Allow Windows backup on devices through the settings catalog so there is something to restore.
  3. Use user-driven Autopilot; restore does not run in self-deploying mode or on hybrid joined devices.

What users notice: On a new device people are offered their wallpaper, settings and pinned apps from the old one.

UX-015 Password reset from the Windows sign-in screen, and back to AD for synced users

What We Found
  • Password reset on the Windows sign-in screen: no
  • Synced users need password writeback: no
  • Password writeback on: no
Why It Matters

Self-service reset helps only if people can reach it. A person who forgot their password is usually stuck at the Windows sign-in screen, not in a browser; the reset link there turns a help desk call into two minutes. For synced accounts, writeback makes that reset count in AD as well.

How To Fix
  1. In a settings catalog profile for Windows, set Authentication, Allow Aad Password Reset to Allowed, so the sign-in screen shows Reset password.
  2. For synced users, turn on password writeback in Entra Connect or Cloud Sync, so a reset in the cloud changes the AD password too.

What users notice: Someone locked out of their laptop can reset their password from the Windows sign-in screen with their MFA methods, and for synced users the new password works on-premises too.

Why It Matters

Licences assigned one person at a time wait for someone to remember them: new starters sit without Teams or Outlook, leavers keep paid licences. Group-based licensing ties the licence to the group, so joining, moving and leaving take care of it.

How To Fix
  1. Create a group per licence package (dynamic on department or job, or fed by HR provisioning) and assign the licences to the group in the Microsoft 365 admin center or Entra.
  2. Move people over by adding them to the group, then remove the direct assignment.

What We Found

2 affected.

Affected (2)
  • RFI Triage Agent (agent identity with no sponsor)
  • Tender Research Pilot (agent identity with no sponsor)
Why It Matters

An owner keeps an agent running; a sponsor answers for it. The sponsor is who is asked whether the agent is still needed, whether its access is still right, and what to do when it misbehaves. Without one, an access review of the agent has nobody to go to and the agent outlives the project it was made for. This check counts sponsors on agent identities, agent blueprints and the blueprints' service principals.

How To Fix

  2. A sponsor can be a group, which keeps the role filled when one person moves on.
  3. With Entra ID Governance, a lifecycle workflow can hand an agent's sponsorship to the sponsor's manager when the sponsor leaves.

What users notice: Nothing changes for people.

What We Found
  • Intune role assignments over every device and user: 1

Affected (1)

Why It Matters

Intune has its own roles beside the Entra ones, and each assignment says which devices and users it reaches. An assignment over all devices and all users gives a team, often the help desk, the same reach as a tenant administrator for whatever the role allows: wiping, retiring, reading recovery keys. ID-044 Application certificates are valid for no longer than 180 days

What We Found
  • App registrations with a certificate valid past the limit: 1
  • Days an application certificate may be valid, at most: 180

1 affected.

Affected (1)
  • Intranet Search (a certificate valid for 730 days (limit 180))
Why It Matters

A certificate that is valid for years is a credential nobody has to think about for years, including after its private key was copied. A short life forces rotation into a routine and bounds how long a stolen key works. The applications listed hold a certificate valid for longer than the limit from start to end.

How To Fix
  1. For each application listed, issue a new certificate valid for 180 days or less and add it to the registration.

CA-021 Unknown device platforms are blocked

What We Found
  • Policies that block unknown device platforms: 0
Why It Matters

Your device rules are written per platform: compliant Windows, managed iPhones. A platform nobody wrote a rule for meets none of them. An attacker's tooling can claim to be any platform it likes, and the ones with no rule are the ones it picks.

How To Fix
  1. Read the sign-in log for the device platforms people really use.
  2. Create a Conditional Access policy for all users and all resources: Device platforms, include Any device, exclude the platforms you support, grant Block access.
  3. Start in report-only mode and exclude the break-glass accounts.

What users notice: A sign-in from a platform you did not list, often Linux or ChromeOS, is refused. People on those platforms need an exception or a supported device.

Why It Matters

This is the middle setting: people can still read and edit in a browser, and the file never lands on a disk you cannot wipe. It takes effect only when both halves are set, the policy here and the unmanaged devices setting in SharePoint.

Licensing

What the tenant holds, what is switched on, what each security goal needs, and the combination of licences that covers the goals. Take the answer to your Microsoft partner.

What To Add

For the core goals (set your own with New-PostureProfile -Goal): Phishing-resistant sign-in enforced; Risky sign-ins challenged, compromised accounts contained; Administrator roles just in time; Only compliant devices reach company data; A device under attack loses access; Endpoint detection and automated response; Phishing and malware stopped in mail, Teams and Office; Sensitive files labelled and encrypted.

Change the goals or the products you already use
Goals
Covered by another product

Nothing here is saved. To keep a change, set it in the profile: New-PostureProfile -Goal ... -ThirdParty @{ edr = 'CrowdStrike' }.

Covered. The licences you hold include every feature these goals need. The work is configuration: see Recommendations.

A starting point to take to your Microsoft partner, not licensing advice. Each licence is named for what it covers. Eligibility and terms are your partner's to confirm, and some add-ons need a base licence.
